declaracion.title: Authenticity Declaration
declaracion.guidance:
The Authenticity Declaration certifies that the work is original

"I declare that this thesis is original and my own work.
All sources consulted have been duly cited and referenced
in accordance with APA 7th edition standards."
Some faculties and programs additionally require:

Verify the requirements with your program — the form may be required

resumen.title: Abstract
resumen.guidance:
Abstract in Spanish. Recommended: 200–350 words.
Must be self-contained: no citations, no undefined abbreviations, no equations.
Recommended structure per APA 7th edition:
  1. Research problem statement.
  2. General objective(s) of the study.
  3. Methodological approach and research design.
  4. Main findings or results.
  5. Conclusions and contributions to the field.
End with 4 to 6 Keywords separated by semicolons.
The abstract will appear in the UNAM Library System catalog
(UNAM Biblioweb) — write it as a standalone piece.

abstract_ingles.title: Abstract

introduccion.title: Introduction
introduccion.label: capitulo:introduccion
introduccion.guidance:
The introduction establishes the context, the problem and the contribution.
Structure recommended by UNAM-CEP for graduate theses:
1. Contextualization: overview of the field of study.
2. Problem statement: what gap or contradiction exists in current knowledge?
3. Rationale: why is it relevant to address it? (theoretical, practical
   or social importance).
4. Research question(s): stated precisely.
5. General objective and specific objectives: concrete and measurable.
6. Hypothesis or working assumption (if applicable to the research design).
7. Scope: spatial, temporal and thematic boundaries of the study.
8. Thesis structure: a brief paragraph per chapter.
APA 7 citations: (Author, year) in the text or Author (year) in narrative form.
Typical length: 15–25 pages.

marco_teorico.title: Theoretical Framework and Literature Review
marco_teorico.label: capitulo:marcoteorico
marco_teorico.guidance:
The theoretical framework presents the conceptual foundations and state of the art.
CEP-UNAM guidelines:
• Organize by theoretical currents, approaches or debates — not as a
  sequential summary of authors.
• Define the key concepts you will use throughout the thesis.
• Review the most relevant literature (last 10 years, plus foundational works).
• Identify contradictions, gaps and unresolved debates that
  justify your research.
• Conclude by explicitly positioning your work within the field.
APA 7 citations: every claim about existing literature requires a citation.
For secondary citations, use: "as cited in Author (year)".
Typical length: 30–60 pages.

marco_conceptual.title: Conceptual Framework
marco_conceptual.label: capitulo:marcoconceptual
marco_conceptual.guidance:
Optional. Activate as an independent chapter if your thesis requires
developing a novel analytical framework or if the theoretical contribution
is central to the research.
Includes: operational definition of variables or analytical categories,
conceptual relationships, and the author’s own model or analytical scheme.
In many social science and humanities theses, the conceptual framework
is integrated within the Theoretical Framework chapter.

metodologia.title: Methodology
metodologia.label: capitulo:metodologia
metodologia.guidance:
The methodology must allow the study to be replicated. Includes:
• Approach and paradigm: quantitative, qualitative or mixed. Justify
  the choice based on the problem and research questions.
• Research design: experimental, quasi-experimental, correlational,
  descriptive, phenomenological, hermeneutic, etc.
• Units of analysis, population and sample (or corpus): selection
  criteria, size, sampling procedure.
• Data collection instruments and techniques: surveys, interviews,
  observation, documentary analysis, content analysis, etc.
  Include information about instrument validation.
• Data analysis procedure: software used (SPSS, R, Atlas.TI, NVivo),
  statistical or analytical techniques.
• Ethical considerations: Ethics Committee approval if human subjects
  were involved; informed consent.
• Methodological limitations.
APA 7: standardized assessment instruments require a full citation.

resultados.title: Results
resultados.label: capitulo:resultados
resultados.guidance:
Present findings objectively, without interpretation.
• Organize by research question or specific objective.
• For quantitative studies: report descriptive statistics,
  hypothesis test results (statistic, p-value, effect size),
  confidence intervals. Tables and figures with footnotes per APA 7.
• For qualitative studies: present emerging categories or themes
  with representative verbatim quotes; ensure participant anonymization
  as committed to in the informed consent.
• Every table and figure must be referenced in the text before it appears.
• APA 7: “Table X shows…”, “Figure X illustrates…”
Length: varies; in quantitative theses often 30–60 pages.

discusion.title: Discussion
discusion.label: capitulo:discusion
discusion.guidance:
Interpret results in relation to the theoretical framework and literature.
APA 7 recommends opening with a statement of support or non-support for the hypothesis.
A solid discussion:
• Takes each result and connects it to theory and prior evidence
  (confirming, contradicting or nuancing it).
• Explains unexpected or contradictory results.
• Discusses theoretical and practical implications.
• Honestly acknowledges the study’s limitations.
• Suggests specific future research directions, derived from
  limitations and unresolved findings.
In many UNAM theses this chapter is merged with Results or Conclusions.
Activate as an independent chapter if the analysis warrants it.

conclusiones.title: Conclusions
conclusiones.label: capitulo:conclusiones
conclusiones.guidance:
Conclusions synthesize the central argument and contributions:
• Directly answer each research question or objective.
• Summarize original contributions: what does the field now know that
  it did not know before this research?
• Practical, public policy or management implications (if applicable).
• Specific and honest limitations of the work.
• Concrete and bounded future research directions.
Avoid repeating results — the committee has read the previous chapter.
In UNAM doctoral theses the committee will evaluate an oral defense;
conclusions are the text that best prepares that conversation.
Typical length: 10–20 pages.

referencias.title: References
referencias.guidance:
APA 7th edition: alphabetical list by first author’s last name,
hanging indent, generated automatically from your .bib file.
APA 7 verification points:
• Book and journal titles in italics.
• Article and chapter titles without quotation marks (unlike APA 6).
• DOI in URL format: https://doi.org/xxxxx (no trailing period).
• For online sources: include URL and access date if content may change.
• For unpublished theses: Last, N. (Year). Thesis title
  [Doctoral dissertation, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México].
Expected volume for doctoral theses: 100–300 references.

apendices.title: Appendices
apendices.guidance:
Supplementary materials that would interrupt the main narrative:
• Research instruments (questionnaires, interview guides,
  observation rubrics).
• Raw data, extended statistical tables or additional results.
• Ethics Committee approval letter and consent forms.
• Interview transcripts (representative excerpts).
• Authorization letters from collaborating institutions.
Label: Appendix A, B… with descriptive title.
Reference from the text: "(see Appendix A)".

introduccion.title: Introduction and Background
introduccion.label: capitulo:introduccion
introduccion.guidance:
In health sciences, the Introduction and Background are typically
a single chapter or adjacent sections. Includes:
1. Epidemiological context: prevalence, incidence, disease burden,
   relevance in the Mexican and global context.
2. Pathophysiology or conceptual framework of the disease/clinical problem.
3. State of the art: critical review of the most relevant literature
   (last 5–10 years + foundational works).
   Vancouver: numerical citations in order of appearance [1], [2].
4. Problem statement: what knowledge gap or unresolved clinical problem
   justifies this thesis?
5. Rationale: clinical, epidemiological or scientific relevance.
6. Hypothesis (if applicable to the design).
7. General objective and specific objectives.
Vancouver: the first citation of a source takes its number; if cited again,
use the same original number.
Typical length: 15–30 pages.

planteamiento.title: Theoretical Framework
planteamiento.label: capitulo:marcoteorico
planteamiento.guidance:
Optional. For basic science or biomedical theses with a relevant theoretical
component (biochemistry, pharmacology, genetics, biostatistics).
Develops the theoretical foundations of the biological model, molecular
mechanism, or analytical methodology underpinning the thesis.
In many clinical theses this content is integrated into the Introduction.

materiales_metodos.title: Materials and Methods
materiales_metodos.label: capitulo:metodos
materiales_metodos.guidance:
Critical section for reproducibility. ICMJE structure:
• Study design: observational (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional),
  experimental (RCT, pre-post, time series), or qualitative.
  Justify the choice.
• Setting and period: hospital, clinic, laboratory; start and
  end dates of data collection.
• Population: inclusion and exclusion criteria, operational definition
  of cases.
• Sample: sample size calculated with an explicit formula, confidence
  level, power and parameters used. Sampling type.
• Variables: operational definition, type (continuous/discrete
  quantitative, nominal/ordinal qualitative) and units of measurement.
• Intervention or exposure (if applicable): precise and reproducible description.
• Instruments and techniques: validated or standardized with their references.
• Statistical analysis: software (SPSS, Stata, R, MedCalc, GraphPad),
  statistical tests with justification (parametric/non-parametric),
  significance level (generally α = 0.05).
• Ethical considerations: Ethics and Research Committee (CEI) registration
  number, COFEPRIS registration if applicable,
  ClinicalTrials.gov registration (if RCT), informed consent.
Typical length: 10–20 pages.

resultados.title: Results
resultados.label: capitulo:resultados
resultados.guidance:
Present findings objectively and in order, without interpretation.
• Begin with sociodemographic characteristics of the population
  (Table 1 with baseline characteristics).
• Report results in the order of the specific objectives.
• Quantitative: report mean ± SD or median (IQR) according to distribution;
  comparisons with statistic, p-value and effect size; 95% CI.
  Use tables for extensive numerical data and figures for trends.
• Qualitative: present thematic categories with representative verbatims.
• All tables and figures must be numbered sequentially and
  referenced in the text before they appear.
• Vancouver: each table has a brief title above; each figure has
  a detailed legend below.
Typical length: 15–40 pages.

discusion.title: Discussion
discusion.label: capitulo:discusion
discusion.guidance:
The discussion interprets results in the context of the literature.
ICMJE recommended structure for biomedical discussions:
1. Summary of the main finding (first sentence of the discussion).
2. Comparison with similar studies: do they confirm, contradict or nuance
   your results? What explains discrepancies?
3. Proposed mechanisms: how do you biologically or clinically explain
   the observed findings?
4. Clinical implications: what changes in medical practice?
   (Be conservative — avoid claims not supported by evidence.)
5. Study limitations: selection bias, information bias, residual confounding,
   sample size, generalizability.
   Be specific and honest — reviewers and committees always look for them.
6. Strengths of the study.
7. Future research: questions that remain unanswered.
Typical length: 15–30 pages.

conclusiones.title: Conclusions
conclusiones.label: capitulo:conclusiones
conclusiones.guidance:
Conclusions directly answer the specific objectives.
Each conclusion must:
• Derive directly from the results (no unsupported inferences).
• Be written in declarative affirmative or negative language.
• Include the level of certainty if applicable (e.g., results suggest,
  it was demonstrated, no significant difference was found).
Avoid concluding beyond what the data allow.
Briefly add practical or public health recommendations
if the evidence justifies it.
Typical length: 1–5 pages (health science conclusions tend to be
more concise than in social sciences).

referencias.title: References
referencias.guidance:
Vancouver style (ICMJE): numbered in order of first appearance in the text.
Generated automatically from your .bib file by biber/biblatex-vancouver.
Standard entry format:
• Article: Last N, Last N. Article title.
  Abbreviated J Name. year;vol(num):pp–pp. DOI or PMID.
• Book: Last N. Title. City: Publisher; year. p. pp.
• Chapter: Last N. Chapter title. In: Editor A, editor.
  Book title. City: Publisher; year. p. pp–pp.
Journal abbreviations: use the Index Medicus / PubMed list.
DOI mandatory when available; if not, URL + access date.
ICMJE recommended maximum for articles: 30–40 refs.
Theses: no strict limit; typically 60–150 references.

apendices.title: Appendices
apendices.guidance:
Supplementary materials:
• Ethics and Research Committee opinion.
• Informed consent form (final approved version).
• Data collection instruments: questionnaires, scales, capture forms.
• ClinicalTrials.gov registration or equivalent (if applicable).
• Extended data tables or sensitivity analysis results.
• Authorization from the institution where the study was conducted.
Label: Appendix A, B… with descriptive title.

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.label: chapter:introduction
introduction.guidance:
The introduction establishes the intellectual context and stakes of your dissertation. It must:
1. Define the research problem with precision — what gap in knowledge does this address?
2. Situate your work within the existing literature (brief synthesis — the full review is later).
3. State your research questions or hypotheses explicitly.
4. Describe your theoretical framework and methodological approach.
5. Articulate the dissertation's original contribution.
6. Outline the chapter structure.
Harvard dissertations are read by a committee of experts — they expect scholarly precision
from the first paragraph. Avoid starting broad; engage the specific problem immediately.
Length: 15–30 pages typical.

literature_review.title: Literature Review
literature_review.label: chapter:literature
literature_review.guidance:
The literature review demonstrates mastery of the field and positions your contribution.
Harvard GSAS expectations:
• Organize thematically or methodologically, not as a sequential summary of papers.
• Identify schools of thought, debates, and key theoretical divides.
• Critically evaluate — what each approach does and fails to do.
• Build explicitly toward the gap your dissertation fills.
• Cover major journals and recent (last 5–10 years) scholarship; foundational works can be older.
Use the DOI importer to add papers from Crossref. Zotero integration is available for
importing directly from your library.
Length: 30–60 pages for a humanities or social science dissertation.

theoretical_framework.title: Theoretical Framework
theoretical_framework.label: chapter:theory
theoretical_framework.guidance:
Develop the theoretical lens through which you analyze your data or argument.
Explain: what theory you adopt, why it is the right tool for your research questions,
and how you operationalize key concepts.
In many disciplines this is integrated into the Literature Review or Methodology.
Activate as a separate chapter if your theoretical contribution is substantial.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.label: chapter:methodology
methodology.guidance:
The methodology chapter must provide enough detail for replication. Include:
• Research design and paradigm (positivist, interpretivist, critical, mixed).
• Data collection: sources, selection criteria, sample size, instruments.
• Data analysis: procedures, software, analytic framework, validity checks.
• Positionality if relevant (qualitative research).
• Ethical approval: if human subjects were involved, include IRB approval information.
• Limitations of the methodology.
The committee will scrutinize this chapter for rigor — be precise about choices made.

results.title: Results / Findings
results.label: chapter:results
results.guidance: Present your findings objectively and organize them by question, objective, or topic. Use tables and figures when they improve clarity.

discussion.title: Discussion
discussion.label: chapter:discussion
discussion.guidance:
The discussion interprets findings in relation to theory and prior literature.
A strong Harvard dissertation discussion:
• Opens by restating the research question and summarizing the key finding.
• Connects each finding to the existing literature (confirming, contradicting, extending).
• Explains unexpected results with theoretical grounding.
• Discusses implications: theoretical (what this means for the field) and practical.
• Acknowledges limitations honestly — the committee will find them anyway.
• Suggests specific future directions tied to the limitations you identify.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.label: chapter:conclusion
conclusion.guidance:
The conclusion synthesizes the dissertation's argument and contribution.
• Directly answer each research question or verify each hypothesis.
• State the original contribution clearly — what does the field now know that it did not before?
• Broader implications: how does this change practice, policy, or theory?
• Concrete, actionable future research directions.
Avoid merely summarizing chapters — the committee has read them.
Length: 10–20 pages.

• Survey instruments, interview guides, or data collection protocols.
• Extended data tables or additional statistical outputs.
• IRB approval letter and consent forms.
• Large code bases or algorithms (if not in the main text).
Label: Appendix A, Appendix B… with descriptive titles.

In humanities dissertations this chapter is typically called "Historiography,"
"State of the Field," or "Theoretical and Methodological Foundations."
Rename the chapter title to match your discipline's conventions.
Harvard GSAS expectations:
• Organize thematically, by school of thought, or by methodology —
 never as a chronological summary of "what each scholar said."
• Identify the major interpretive debates and your position within them.
• Critically engage prior work: where it succeeds, where it falls short,
 and why this dissertation's approach is necessary.
• Introduce the theoretical frameworks you employ (e.g., subaltern studies,
 memory theory, critical race theory, new historicism) and justify their use.
• Be ruthlessly selective — cite the most significant work, not everything.
Chicago 17: cite primary sources and secondary literature in footnotes.
For archival work, introduce your primary source base here or in the next chapter.
Length: 20–50 pages depending on scope.

theoretical_framework.title: Theoretical Framework
theoretical_framework.label: chapter:theory
theoretical_framework.guidance:

philosophy, literary theory, postcolonial studies).
Develop your theoretical lens: what framework(s) do you employ, why are they
appropriate for your object of study, and how do you operationalize key concepts?
Acknowledge the framework's limitations and potential critiques.
In many humanities dissertations this is woven into the Introduction or the
Historiography chapter — activate as a standalone chapter only when your
theoretical contribution is itself part of the original argument.

methodology.label: chapter:methodology
methodology.guidance: Details the research design, data or sample, instruments, procedure, analysis strategy, tools, and ethical considerations with sufficient detail to replicate the study.

results.title: Chapter Two
results.label: chapter:two
results.guidance:
Rename this section to your second chapter's actual title (e.g., "The Archive
of Silence: Memory and State Violence, 1936–1945").
In humanities dissertations, body chapters present the dissertation's argument
through sustained engagement with primary sources. Each chapter should:
• Open with a clear statement of the chapter's argument and its relationship
 to the dissertation's overall thesis.
• Develop a specific aspect of the larger argument through close analysis.
• Engage primary sources (archival documents, literary texts, images, oral
 testimonies) in depth — not as illustration but as evidence.
• Engage the relevant secondary literature in footnotes or in the body text.
• Close by connecting the chapter's findings to the broader argument and
 pointing forward to the next chapter.
Chicago 17 footnotes: use to cite, to add commentary that would interrupt
the main argument, or to acknowledge alternative interpretations.
Typical chapter length: 40–70 pages.

discussion.title: Chapter Three
discussion.label: chapter:three
discussion.guidance:
Rename to your third chapter's actual title.
See guidance for Chapter Two — the same structural principles apply.
Additional considerations for middle chapters:
• Each chapter must stand alone as a coherent argument and also function
 as part of the dissertation's larger arc.
• Transitions between chapters matter: the conclusion of each chapter should
 anticipate the next.
• Avoid repeating material from earlier chapters — assume your reader has
 read them.
Activate additional chapters (Chapters Four, Five, etc.) using the Appendices
section or by duplicating this section. Dissertations in history and literature
typically have 4–6 body chapters.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.label: chapter:conclusion
conclusion.guidance:
The conclusion advances the argument — it does not merely summarize the chapters.
A strong Harvard humanities conclusion:
• Restates the dissertation's central claim now enriched by the evidence
 presented across all chapters.
• Synthesizes the implications: what does this argument mean for the field,
 for related fields, or for broader public debates?
• Opens outward: suggests new questions, problems, or archives that this
 dissertation reveals but does not resolve.
• Briefly sketches the path to publication — committees will ask which
 chapters are being developed for journals or which press you are targeting.
Avoid restating chapter summaries — the committee has read the dissertation.
Length: 10–25 pages.

methodology.title: Research Design
methodology.label: chapter:methodology
methodology.guidance:

"Empirical Strategy," or "Case Selection and Method."
This chapter must establish the credibility of your causal claims. Include:
• Research design: observational, quasi-experimental, experimental, or
 interpretive. Justify why this design answers your research question.
• Case selection: logic of case choice; typicality, variation, or
 representativeness as appropriate.
• Data: sources, collection procedures, sample characteristics, and
 any collection instruments.
• Analytic method: regression, process tracing, comparetive-historical,
 discourse analysis, etc. Justify choices and acknowledge limitations.
• Identification strategy: how do you address confounding, endogeneity,
 or selection bias?
• IRB/ethical approval if human subjects research.

• Report main results with statistical significance, effect sizes, and
 confidence intervals.
• Present robustness checks and sensitivity analyses.
• Include Tables and Figures with clear captions; reference each in the text.
For qualitative/interpretive dissertations:
• Present cases or themes systematically, with primary source evidence.
• Tie each piece of evidence to the analytical framework.

• Why do unexpected results occur?

conceptually substantial.

• Summarize the key empirical contributions and their theoretical implications.
• Address scope conditions: where and when do your findings apply?
• Policy implications (where relevant to your field).
• Future research: specific questions opened by your findings that require

Do not merely restate chapter summaries — advance the argument.

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.label: chapter:introduction
introduction.guidance: Presents the context, problem statement, justification, research questions, objectives, scope and structure of the document.

background.title: Background and Related Work
background.label: chapter:background
background.guidance: Review relevant literature and theoretical foundations. Organize by themes or debates and identify the gap that your work addresses.

methodology.title: Proposed Approach
methodology.label: chapter:methodology
methodology.guidance:
Core technical contribution with full reproducibility:
• Problem formulation: mathematical or formal definition.
• System design or algorithm description (with block diagrams).
• Theoretical analysis: complexity, bounds, or convergence proofs.
• Key design decisions and their justifiestion.
• Implementation details relevant to correctness.
TUM technical committees (Prüfungskommission) include external expert
examiners — the contribution must be unambiguously stated and proven.

experiments.title: Experimental Evaluation
experiments.label: chapter:experiments
experiments.guidance:
TUM committees apply strong experimental standards. Include:
• Experimental setup: hardware, software environment, datasets, baselines,
 metrics, and hyperparameters.
• Ablation studies for each major design decision.
• Comparison to the strongest relevant baselines.
• Statistical significance: report mean ± std, or confidence intervals.
• Failure analysis.
Industry relevance: if the thesis has industrial motivation, include
evaluation on realistic or industry-standard benchmarks.
IEEE: "Fig. X" and "Table X" in text. Vector graphics for all plots.

discussion.title: Discussion
discussion.label: chapter:discussion
discussion.guidance:
Interpret results beyond raw numbers:
• Why does the proposed approach work?
• Where does it fail? Honest failure analysis.
• Industrial applicability and scalability.
• Comparison to the state of the art in the broader context.
Often merged with Experimental Evaluation or Conclusion in TUM theses.

conclusion.title: Conclusion and Outlook
conclusion.label: chapter:conclusion
conclusion.guidance:
Close with precision:
• Restate contributions — what the field now knows scholarshipuse of this thesis.
• Summarize key experimental results supporting each contribution.
• Limitations: specific and honest.
• Outlook (Ausblick): concrete future research directions.
• List publications arising from the thesis (Veröffentlichungen im Rahmen
 dieser Arbeit) — TUM Promotionsbüro may require a publications list.
Length: 5–15 pages.

references.title: References
references.guidance: Include only the cited sources and follow the bibliographic style required by the profile.

appendices.title: Appendices
appendices.guidance:
Supplementary technical material:
• Extended proofs or mathematical derivations.
• Full algorithm listings.
• Additional experimental results.
• Dataset descriptions and preprocessing pipelines.
• Code availability: GitHub/GitLab URL or TUM Data Repository.
Label: Appendix A, B… Cross-reference from the main text.

propositions.title: Propositions (Stellingen)
propositions.guidance:
The Stellingen (Propositions) are a defining feature of Dutch PhD dissertations.
TU Delft requires 10 propositions accompanying the dissertation, submitted
separately but printed as a loose sheet distributed at the defence.
Requirements:
• 10 propositions total.
• At least 5 must be directly related to the dissertation topic.
• The remaining propositions may be from the candidate's field or broader
 academic/societal topics (these stimulate discussion at the defence).
• Must be approved by the promotor(s) before submission.
Note: in TeXisStudio, the propositions are authored separately and not
compiled into the main PDF — use this section for drafting only.

summary.title: Summary
summary.guidance:
English summary of the dissertation. Required by TU Delft for all PhD theses.
Typically 1–2 pages (500–1000 words).
Structure:
 1. Research problem and motivation.
 2. Approach and methodology.
 3. Key findings and contributions.
 4. Significance for the field.
The summary appears in the thesis and is submitted to the TU Delft
repository (Institutional Repository) and ProQuest.

If Dutch is not your first language, it is standard to have a native speaker

experiments.title: Experimental Evaluation

Experimental rigor is expected by TU Delft committees. Include:
• Experimental setup: hardware, datasets (with statistics), baselines,
 metrics, and hyperparameters.
• Ablation studies for major design decisions.
• Comparison against the strongest relevant baselines.
• Statistical reliability: mean ± std, confidence intervals, or
 significance tests across multiple runs.
• Honest failure analysis.
TU Delft values both fundamental results and practical applicability.
Include validation on real-world or industrially relevant benchmarks
where your research has practical motivation.

discussion.title: Discussion

discussion.guidance:
Interpret results in broader context:
• Why does the method work? Theoretical intuition.

• Scalability and generalisability.

Often merged with Experimental Evaluation in TU Delft engineering theses.

conclusion.title: Conclusions and Recommendations

• Limitations: specific and honest.

 tied to your open questions and limitations.
• Valorisation: TU Delft encourages a brief note on the societal and
 economic value of the research (relevant for industry-funded PhDs).
• List publications arising from the thesis — required for the TU Delft
 repository record.
Length: 5–15 pages.

Cambridge Graduate Office requires the following elements on the title page:

• Your full name as registered with the University.
• College name.
• Degree for which it is submitted (e.g. "Doctor of Philosophy").
• Month and year of submission.

No page number on this page.

declaration.title: Declaration
declaration.guidance:
Cambridge requires a signed declaration that the thesis is your own work.
Required text (Cambridge Graduate Office):
 "This thesis is the result of my own work and includes nothing which is the
  outcome of work done in collaboration except as declared in the Preface and
  specified in the text. It is not substantially the same as any that I have
  submitted, or am submitting, for a degree or diploma or other qualification
  at the University of Cambridge or any other University or similar institution
  [...]. It does not exceed the prescribed word limit for the relevant Degree
  Committee."
Adapt the bracketed text per your Degree Committee's specific wording.
Word limit statement: include your actual word count.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.guidance: Write a self-contained summary with problem, objective, method, main results and contribution. Respect the required length and add keywords if requested.

acknowledgements.title: Acknowledgements
acknowledgements.guidance:

collaborators, and any third-party data or material providers.
If your research involved human subjects, acknowledge ethics approval here
(e.g. "This research was approved by the Cambridge Psychology Research Ethics
Committee, reference PREC/2023/xxx").
Typical length: half to one page.

table_of_contents.title: Table of Contents
table_of_contents.guidance:
Auto-generated from chapter and section headings.
Should list all front matter, chapters, and back matter with page numbers.
List of Figures and List of Tables are optional but recommended if you have
more than 5 figures or tables respectively.

abbreviations.title: List of Abbreviations
abbreviations.guidance:

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.label: ch:introduction
introduction.guidance:
The introduction must establish:
1. The research problem and its significance in the field.
2. The gap in existing knowledge that your thesis addresses.
3. Your research questions or hypotheses.
4. The original contribution to knowledge (Cambridge examiners will test this directly).
5. Scope and limitations.
6. Chapter outline.
Cambridge PhD examiners expect you to articulate what is NEW in your work.
Typical length: 8–15 pages (varies by discipline).
Word limit for the entire PhD thesis: 80,000 words (excluding bibliography,
appendices, tables, and figures) for most Degree Committees.
Check your specific Degree Committee's regulations — some faculties differ.

literature_review.title: Literature Review
literature_review.label: ch:literature
literature_review.guidance:
A Cambridge PhD literature review demonstrates command of the field.
Expected depth: systematic coverage of work from the last 5–10 years,
plus seminal older works.
Structure critically — do not summarise paper by paper. Instead:
• Group by theme, methodology, or chronological development.
• Critique each strand: what it shows and what it leaves unresolved.
• Build to the gap statement that motivates your research.
Recommended sources: Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO, JSTOR.
Use the DOI importer in TeXisStudio to cite articles correctly in APA 7.
Tip: Cambridge examiners read the literature review to assess whether you
know the field better than any single published paper in it.

theoretical_framework.title: Theoretical Framework
theoretical_framework.label: ch:theory
theoretical_framework.guidance:
Develop the conceptual or theoretical foundation of your research.
Relevant for social science, humanities, or interdisciplinary PhDs.
Distinguish clearly between theoretical framework (the lens you use)
and literature review (the empirical context).
Include: key theoretical concepts, their definitions as you use them,
and why this framework is appropriate for your research questions.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.label: ch:methodology
methodology.guidance: Details the research design, data or sample, instruments, procedure, analysis strategy, tools, and ethical considerations with sufficient detail to replicate the study.

results.title: Results
results.label: ch:results
results.guidance: Present your findings objectively and organize them by question, objective, or topic. Use tables and figures when they improve clarity.

discussion.title: Discussion
discussion.label: ch:discussion
discussion.guidance:
Interpret your results in relation to your research questions and the literature.
A strong Cambridge PhD discussion:
• Addresses each research question/hypothesis directly.
• Situates findings within the broader literature — agree, disagree, extend.
• Offers a theoretical account of unexpected results.
• Discusses practical and theoretical implications.
• Acknowledges limitations honestly — examiners credit intellectual honesty.
• Discusses threats to validity and generalisability.
Avoid merely re-stating results. The discussion is where you demonstrate
your capacity for independent scholarly reasoning.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.label: ch:conclusion
conclusion.guidance:
Synthesise the thesis rather than summarise it.
• Articulate the original contribution to knowledge — what does your thesis
 now allow the field to say that it could not say before?
• Answer your research questions directly.
• State the practical implications for policy, practice, or future research.
• Propose specific directions for future work.
• End with a closing statement that places your work in the broader context.
Cambridge examiners will read the conclusion to judge originality.
Typical length: 5–10 pages.

references.title: References
references.guidance:
Auto-generated by Biber from your .bib file in APA 7 format.
APA 7 conventions at Cambridge: use DOI when available (mandatory for recent articles).
Do not include works not cited in the text.
For a Cambridge PhD: typically 100–300+ references.
Use the DOI importer in TeXisStudio to add references directly from Crossref.

appendices.title: Appendices
appendices.guidance:
Appendices do NOT count toward the 80,000-word limit.
Include: interview guides, survey instruments, ethics documentation,
supplementary tables, extended code, additional analyses.
Label: Appendix A, Appendix B, etc., each with a descriptive title.
Each appendix should be referenced in the main text.

uk_cambridge_apa7.name: Cambridge - PhD Thesis (APA 7)
uk_cambridge_apa7.description: University of Cambridge PhD thesis for social sciences, psychology, and education. Follows Cambridge Graduate Office format guidelines: A4, 40mm left margin (binding), double-spacing, 12pt, APA 7 bibliography via Biber. Word limit: 80,000 words.

title_page.title: Title Page
title_page.guidance:
Cambridge Graduate Office requires the following elements on the title page:
• Full thesis title.
• Author's full name.
• College name.
• "This dissertation is submitted for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy."
• Month and Year of submission (e.g., "May 2026").
• "This dissertation is the result of my own work and includes nothing
 which is the outcome of work done in collaboration except as declared
 in the Preface and specified in the text." (declaration — may go on
 a separate page).
Cambridge does not have a signature page — your supervisor submits
approval through the CamSIS system.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.guidance: Write a self-contained summary with problem, objective, method, main results and contribution. Respect the required length and add keywords if requested.

acknowledgements.title: Acknowledgements
acknowledgements.guidance:
Acknowledge: supervisor(s) and PhD committee, departmental colleagues,
funding bodies (mandatory — include grant numbers).
EPSRC, BBSRC, Wellcome Trust, Royal Society, and EU project numbers
must be cited verbatim as required by the funder.
Example: "This work was funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences
Research Council (EPSRC) under grant EP/X000000/0."
Typical length: half to one page.

table_of_contents.title: Table of Contents
table_of_contents.guidance:
Generated automatically from section headings.
Cambridge requires a complete Table of Contents with accurate page numbers.
Depth: chapters and major sections (levels 1–3 recommended for
technical theses with significant internal structure).

list_of_figures.title: List of Figures
list_of_figures.guidance:
Required if the thesis contains figures. Auto-generated from captions.
Each entry: figure number, abbreviated caption, page number.
Enable if you have 5 or more figures.

list_of_tables.title: List of Tables
list_of_tables.guidance:
Required if the thesis contains tables. Auto-generated from captions.
Enable if you have 5 or more tables.

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.label: chapter:introduction
introduction.guidance: Presents the context, problem statement, justification, research questions, objectives, scope and structure of the document.

background.title: Background and Related Work
background.label: chapter:background
background.guidance: Review relevant literature and theoretical foundations. Organize by themes or debates and identify the gap that your work addresses.

methodology.title: Proposed Methodology
methodology.label: chapter:methodology
methodology.guidance:
The core technical contribution. Must be complete enough for replication:
• Problem formulation: mathematical or computational definition.
• System design or algorithm description (with diagrams where helpful).
• Theoretical analysis: complexity, convergence, correctness, or bounds.
• Key design choices with justifiestion.
• Implementation details relevant to correctness (full listings → Appendix).
Cambridge examiners apply a strict standard: every claim must be stated
as a theorem/proposition/lemma (if formal) or as an empirically testable
hypothesis (if experimental). Ambiguity in the contribution is the most
common reason for major corrections.

experiments.title: Experimental Evaluation
experiments.label: chapter:experiments
experiments.guidance:
Cambridge examiners evaluate experimental rigor closely. Required elements:
• Experimental setup: hardware (GPU model, CPU, RAM), datasets (statistics,
 splits), baselines, evaluation metrics, and all hyperparameters.
• Ablation studies justifying each major design decision.
• Comparison against the strongest baselines — committee members know the
 literature and will notice if a key baseline is absent.
• Statistical reporting: mean ± std over multiple runs, confidence intervals
 or significance tests where appropriate.
• Honest failure analysis: where and why does the method fail?
Figure formatting: vector graphics (PDF/EPS). Tables: booktabs style.
IEEE: "Fig. X" and "Table X" in the text.

discussion.title: Discussion
discussion.label: chapter:discussion
discussion.guidance:
Interpret the results beyond the numbers:
• Why does the approach work? Can you provide theoretical intuition?
• Where does it fail, and what does that reveal about the problem?
• Scalability: how does performance change with data, compute, or problem scale?
• Generalisability: which aspects transfer to related problems?
In many Cambridge engineering theses this is merged with the Experimental
Evaluation or the Conclusion. Activate standalone only when the analytical
depth warrants it.

conclusion.title: Conclusions and Future Work
conclusion.label: chapter:conclusion
conclusion.guidance:
Cambridge examiners read the conclusion carefully — it must match the claims
in the Introduction:
• Restate each contribution with the evidence from the thesis.
 Do not introduce new claims here.
• Honest limitations: be specific about what the method cannot do.
• Future work: concrete, specific directions tied to limitations and
 open questions.
• Publications arising from the thesis: list any papers published or under
 review. Cambridge examiners require this.
Length: 5–15 pages.

references.title: References
references.guidance: Include only the cited sources and follow the bibliographic style required by the profile.

appendices.title: Appendices
appendices.guidance:
Technical material that would interrupt the main narrative:
• Extended proofs or derivations.
• Full algorithm listings or pseudocode.
• Additional experimental results and ablations.
• Dataset documentation or preprocessing pipelines.
• Code availability: repository URL (GitHub, Zenodo, etc.).
 The British Library requires data availability statements.
Label: Appendix A, B… with descriptive titles; cross-reference from the text.

uk_cambridge_ieee.name: Cambridge - Thesis (IEEE)
uk_cambridge_ieee.description: University of Cambridge PhD thesis for engineering and natural sciences, IEEE

title_page.title: Title Page
title_page.guidance:
Oxford Examination Regulations require the title page to include:
• Full title of the thesis.
• Your full name as registered.
• College name.
• Degree for which submitted (e.g. "Doctor of Philosophy").
• Term and year of submission (e.g. "Michaelmas Term 2025").
No student number, no supervisor name on the title page.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.guidance: Write a self-contained summary with problem, objective, method, main results and contribution. Respect the required length and add keywords if requested.

acknowledgements.title: Acknowledgements
acknowledgements.guidance:
Thank your supervisor and co-supervisors, funding bodies (mandatory if funded),
college, department, collaborators, and ethics boards if relevant.
Note your sources of funding (scholarships, grants, project numbers).
Typical length: half a page.

table_of_contents.title: Table of Contents
table_of_contents.guidance:
Auto-generated. Must list all front matter, chapters, and back matter with page numbers.
Include List of Figures and List of Tables if applicable.

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.label: ch:introduction
introduction.guidance:
The DPhil introduction establishes the scholarly context and originality claim.
Must include:
1. Statement of the research problem and its scholarly significance.
2. The specific gap or question your thesis addresses.
3. Your central argument or thesis statement.
4. What is original in your contribution.
5. Scope, limitations, and methodology overview.
6. Structure of the thesis.
Oxford examiners assess whether the thesis "forms a significant contribution to learning."
Word limit for the entire DPhil thesis: 100,000 words
(excluding bibliography, appendices, footnotes).

literature_review.title: Literature Review
literature_review.label: ch:literature
literature_review.guidance: Review relevant literature and theoretical foundations. Organize by themes or debates and identify the gap that your work addresses.

methodology.title: Methodology and Sources
methodology.label: ch:methodology
methodology.guidance:
For humanities DPhil, discuss:
• Primary sources used and their nature (archival, literary, material culture).
• Methodological approach (close reading, archival analysis, comparetive, etc.).
• Languages and translation issues if applicable.
• Scope of sources and justifiestion for selection.
This chapter is mandatory for social science DPhils; optional for some humanities theses.

chapter_1.title: Chapter 1
chapter_1.label: ch:one
chapter_1.guidance: Complete this section in accordance with the profile requirements and current guidelines of your institution.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.label: ch:conclusion
conclusion.guidance:
Synthesise the argument developed across all chapters.
• Restate the central thesis in light of what has been demonstrated.
• Articulate the contribution to knowledge — what does your thesis now allow
 scholars to say or think differently?
• Indicate avenues for further research.
• Oxford examiners (two appointed examiners, one internal, one external) will
 probe the conclusions in the viva voce examination.
Typical length: 4,000–8,000 words.

bibliography.title: Bibliography
bibliography.guidance: Include only the cited sources and follow the bibliographic style required by the profile.

appendices.title: Appendices
appendices.guidance:
Appendices do NOT count toward the word limit.
Include: primary source transcriptions, data tables, interview transcripts,
archival inventories, maps, genealogical tables.
Label: Appendix A, B, C with descriptive titles.
Reference each appendix from the main text.

uk_oxford_mhra.name: Oxford - DPhil Thesis (MHRA)
uk_oxford_mhra.description: University of Oxford DPhil thesis for humanities. Follows Oxford Examination Regulations: A4, 40mm left margin (binding), double-spacing, 12pt, MHRA 3rd edition via Biber. Word limit: 100,000 words (excluding bibliography and appendices).

portada.title: Title Page

Include institution, specialty program name, work title,
author, advisor, city and date. If your hospital, professional college

Summarizes the professional problem addressed, the context, the intervention

indice.title: Table of Contents

introduccion.guidance:
Presents the professional or clinical problem, the institutional context,

marco_referencial.title: Reference Framework
marco_referencial.guidance:
Synthesizes the regulations, prior evidence, protocols, clinical guidelines
or literature that underpin the adopted approach.

metodologia.title: Methodology / Intervention
metodologia.guidance:
Describes the work design, procedure, selection criteria,
instruments, applied intervention or strategy, and ethical considerations.

resultados.title: Results
resultados.guidance:
Presents the findings, products, metrics, evaluations or observed results
of the specialty work.

discusion.title: Discussion
discusion.guidance:
Interprets the results, compares them with literature or standards,
acknowledges limitations and highlights practical implications.

conclusiones.title: Conclusions and Recommendations
conclusiones.guidance:
Summarizes the professional contribution of the work, its applied utility
and recommendations for continuity or improvement.

referencias.title: References
referencias.guidance: Final reference list in APA 7. Include only cited sources.

anexos.title: Annexes
anexos.guidance:
Supplementary material: instruments, protocols, forms, extended tables
or supporting technical documentation.

generic_especialidad.name: Generic Specialty Project
generic_especialidad.description: Academic profile for Generic Specialty Project. Follow the profile metadata, required sections, and bibliography style.

portada.title: Title Page
portada.guidance:
Include the host institution, postdoctoral project or fellowship,

resumen.title: Abstract
resumen.guidance:
Synthesizes the postdoctoral agenda, objectives, methodological approach,
contributions, results and future projections.
Suggested length: 200–350 words.

abstract_ingles.title: Abstract (English)
abstract_ingles.guidance:
Recommended when the postdoctoral report will circulate internationally

indice.title: Table of Contents
indice.guidance: Generated automatically. Review final pagination consistency.

introduccion.title: Introduction
introduccion.guidance:
Presents the research field, the project agenda and the
positioning of the work within the postdoctoral line of research.

estado_arte.title: State of the Art
estado_arte.guidance:
Develops a critical review of the current state of the field,
identifies gaps and justifies the contribution of the postdoctoral work.

metodologia.title: Methodology
metodologia.guidance:
Explains design, corpus or data, procedures, protocols, tools,

conclusiones.title: Conclusions

generic_posdoctorado.name: Generic Postdoctoral Report
generic_posdoctorado.description: Academic profile for Informe Posdoctoral Genérico. Follow the profile metadata, required sections, and bibliography style.

portada.title: Title Page
portada.guidance:
The title page must include:
• Logo and name of the institution, faculty or school.
• Full title of the tesina (clear and specific).
• "TESINA" and the degree or certificate sought
  (e.g., "to obtain the title of Bachelor in [field]").
• Author’s full name.
• Advisor’s or director’s name.
• City, month and year.
Consult the official title page format of your program.

resumen.title: Abstract
resumen.guidance:
Brief abstract of the tesina. 150–300 words.
Includes: the topic, the objective, the method used, the main
findings and the central conclusion or contribution.
End with 4–6 Keywords.
No citations, no figures, no undefined acronyms.

agradecimientos.title: Acknowledgements
agradecimientos.guidance:
Optional. Thank your advisor, those who provided access to data
or information, and personal support received.
Typical length: one paragraph or half a page.

indice.title: Table of Contents
indice.guidance:
Generated automatically. Includes all chapters and sections
with their page numbers.

introduccion.title: Introduction
introduccion.label: capitulo:introduccion
introduccion.guidance:
The introduction situates the topic and justifies the work.
Includes:
1. Topic presentation: what is the tesina about?
2. Relevance: why is this topic important?
3. Central question or purpose of the work.
4. Objective(s) of the study.
5. Brief description of the tesina’s structure.
Typical length: 3–8 pages.

desarrollo.title: Development
desarrollo.label: capitulo:desarrollo
desarrollo.guidance:
The development is the main body of the tesina. You can structure it
in the following ways depending on the type of work:
Theoretical tesina / academic essay:
  • Review and critical analysis of the relevant literature.
  • Development of the central argument or position with bibliographic support.
  • Discussion of different perspectives or approaches.
Empirical research tesina (small scale):
  • Brief theoretical framework.
  • Methodology: design, sample, instruments, procedure.
  • Results and analysis.
  • Discussion of findings.
Design or project tesina:
  • Diagnosis or problem justification.
  • Intervention or design proposal.
  • Evaluation or validation.
Divide this chapter into sections with clear subheadings.
APA 7: cite with (Author, year) or Author (year).
Typical length: 25–60 pages.

conclusiones.title: Conclusions
conclusiones.label: capitulo:conclusiones
conclusiones.guidance:
Conclusions synthesize what you learned or demonstrated.
• Answer the central question or purpose of the tesina.
• Summarize the main points of the development.
• Note implications or applications.
• Acknowledge the work’s limitations.
• Suggest possible future lines of work or further study.
Typical length: 3–8 pages.
Avoid introducing new information not discussed previously.

referencias.title: References
referencias.guidance:
APA 7th edition: alphabetical list, hanging indent.
Include only sources cited in the text.
Generated automatically from your .bib file.
Include DOI when available.

apendices.title: Appendices
apendices.guidance:
Optional. Additional supporting materials:
• Data collection instruments (if used).
• Extended data tables.
• Additional analysis materials.
Label: Appendix A, B… Reference from the text.

generic_tesina.name: Generic Short Thesis
generic_tesina.description: Academic profile for a generic short thesis. Follow the profile metadata, required sections and bibliography style.

portada.title: Title Page
portada.guidance:
The title page is the first impression of your thesis. Includes:
• Logo and name of your institution (university / faculty / department).
• Full thesis title (informative and specific, no abbreviations).
• Document type: "THESIS" or "DISSERTATION" and the degree sought
  (e.g., "to obtain the degree of Bachelor’s in / Master’s in /
  Doctor’s in [field name]").
• Author’s full name.
• Name of the thesis supervisor or director.
• City, month and year of submission.
Check with your coordinator or program — many institutions have
an official title page format you must follow exactly.

declaracion.title: Authenticity Declaration
declaracion.guidance:
The Authenticity Declaration certifies that the work is yours and that
sources are correctly cited. Standard text (adapt if your institution
has a specific format):
"I declare under oath that this work is original and has been prepared
by the undersigned. All sources consulted have been duly cited and
referenced according to applicable standards."
Some universities require this declaration to be signed, notarized,
or in a specific format — verify with your program.

resumen.title: Abstract
resumen.guidance:
The Spanish abstract is the first academic element other researchers will read.
Recommended: 150–350 words.
APA 7 (for theses and student papers) recommends including:
  1. The research problem (1–2 sentences).
  2. Participants or data used (if applicable).
  3. The methodology or approach used.
  4. The main findings or conclusions.
  5. Implications or contributions of the study.
End with 4–6 Keywords separated by semicolons.
Must be self-contained: no citations, no figures, no undefined acronyms.

abstract_ingles.title: Abstract
abstract_ingles.guidance:
Abstract in English. Optional but recommended for international visibility.
Maximum 350 words. Same structure as the Spanish Abstract.
End with: Keywords: (4–6 terms in English).
Mandatory if your program requires publication in international databases
(Scopus, Web of Science, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses).

agradecimientos.title: Acknowledgements
agradecimientos.guidance:
Optional but conventional section. Acknowledge those who contributed
to your research: thesis supervisor, committee or jury, colleagues,
librarians, study participants, and those who supported you
personally throughout the process.
If your research was funded with a scholarship or external resource
(CONAHCYT, CONACYT, DGAPA, etc.), it is mandatory to mention it with
the project or scholarship number.
Typical length: half to one page.

dedicatoria.title: Dedication
dedicatoria.guidance: Optional. One to three lines. No printed heading.

indice.title: Table of Contents
indice.guidance:
Generated automatically. Includes all front matter (except the title page),
body chapters, appendices and references.
Verify that page numbers are exact before printing.

indice_figuras.title: List of Figures
indice_figuras.guidance:
Enable this section if your thesis has 5 or more figures, graphs or images.
APA 7: number figures continuously (Figure 1, Figure 2…)
and reference them in the text before they appear.

indice_tablas.title: List of Tables
indice_tablas.guidance:
Enable if you have 5 or more tables. APA 7: number tables continuously
(Table 1, Table 2…) and reference them in the text.

introduccion.title: Introduction
introduccion.label: capitulo:introduccion
introduccion.guidance:
The introduction frames your research and convinces the reader of its importance.
Recommended structure:
1. General contextualization of the research topic.
2. Problem statement: what knowledge gap, contradiction
   or practical need does your thesis address?
3. Rationale: why does it matter to resolve it? (theoretical, social,
   economic, clinical, technological relevance, etc.)
4. Research question(s): stated precisely and narrowly.
5. General objective and specific objectives (concrete and measurable).
6. Hypothesis or working assumption (if your design requires it).
7. Scope and delimitations of the study.
8. Thesis structure: a brief paragraph per chapter.
Typical length for undergraduate: 10–20 pages.
For graduate: 15–30 pages.

marco_teorico.title: Theoretical Framework and Literature Review
marco_teorico.label: capitulo:marcoteorico
marco_teorico.guidance:
The theoretical framework is the conceptual foundation of your research. Includes:
• Definition and discussion of the fundamental concepts and theories
  that underpin your work.
• Critical review of the literature: what is known about the topic?
  What are the main approaches? Where are the debates?
• Identification of the gap or contradiction that justifies your study.
• Theoretical positioning: what perspective do you adopt and why?
APA 7: cite with (Author, year) or Author (year) for narrative citations.
For direct quotations include page number: (Author, year, p. xx).
Organize by topics or currents, not as a list of authors.
Typical length: 20–50 pages.

metodologia.title: Methodology
metodologia.label: capitulo:metodologia
metodologia.guidance:
The methodology describes in sufficient detail how you conducted your research.
Includes:
• Approach: quantitative, qualitative or mixed. Justify the choice.
• Research design: experimental, quasi-experimental, correlational,
  descriptive, phenomenological, case study, etc.
• Population and sample (or analysis corpus): selection criteria and size.
• Data collection instruments or techniques: describe each one,
  cite the instrument if published, and indicate if it was adapted or created.
• Data collection procedure: when, where and how data were obtained.
• Data analysis: software used and analysis techniques.
• Ethical considerations: informed consent, confidentiality,
  Ethics Committee approval if human subjects were involved.
• Methodological limitations.
Typical length: 10–25 pages.

resultados.title: Results
resultados.label: capitulo:resultados
resultados.guidance:
Present findings objectively, without interpretation or conclusions.
Organize results according to your research questions or objectives.
For quantitative data:
• Report descriptive statistics first (means, standard deviations, percentages).
• Then inferential tests (t, F, χ², correlations, regressions) with
  their statistics, p-values and effect sizes.
• Include APA 7 tables and figures with footnotes.
For qualitative data:
• Present emerging categories or themes with representative verbatim quotes.
• Ensure participant confidentiality.
APA 7: “Table 1 shows…”, “Figure 2 illustrates…”.
Every table and figure must be mentioned in the text before it appears.

discusion.title: Discussion
discusion.label: capitulo:discusion
discusion.guidance:
The discussion interprets results and connects them to the theoretical
framework and reviewed literature.
Recommended structure:
• First sentence: restate the research question and answer it directly
  based on your results.
• Compare with prior studies: do your findings agree with, contradict or
  nuance existing literature? Why?
• Explain unexpected results.
• Theoretical and practical implications of the findings.
• Study limitations.
• Specific future research suggestions.
In many undergraduate theses this chapter is merged with Results
or Conclusions. Activate as an independent chapter if needed.

conclusiones.title: Conclusions
conclusiones.label: capitulo:conclusiones
conclusiones.guidance:
Conclusions directly answer your research question(s) and objectives.
• Answer each research question or verify each hypothesis.
• Summarize the original contributions of your work to the field.
• Practical implications or possible applications.
• Study limitations (be honest — the committee will find them regardless).
• Future research directions: concrete and bounded.
Do not repeat results — the committee has already read that chapter.
Typical length: 5–15 pages.

referencias.title: References
referencias.guidance:
APA 7th edition: alphabetical list by first author’s last name,
hanging indent. Generated automatically from your .bib file.
Key APA 7 points:
• Italics for book, journal and thesis titles.
• No italics for articles and chapters.
• DOI in URL format: https://doi.org/xxxxx (no trailing period).
• For online sources: URL and access date.
• Thesis: Last, N. (Year). Title [Bachelor’s/Master’s/doctoral thesis,
  University Name]. Repository or database.
Include only sources cited in the body text.

apendices.title: Appendices
apendices.guidance:
Supplementary materials too extensive for the main body
or that would disrupt the narrative flow:
• Complete instruments (questionnaires, scales, interview guides).
• Raw data or additional statistical tables.
• Interview or focus group transcripts.
• Ethics approval letters and informed consent forms.
• Stimulus materials or intervention protocols.
Label: Appendix A, B… with descriptive title.
Reference from the text: "(see Appendix A)".

generic_thesis.description: Academic profile for a generic thesis. Follow the profile metadata, required sections and bibliography style.

company.internship.name: Internship / Residency Report

You don't need to write content here — set the data in the project metadata.

table_of_contents.guidance:
The index is generated automatically.
You don't need to write anything here.

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.guidance:
Contextualize the report and present to the reader the purpose of the practices:
• Career and professional profile of the practitioner.
• Name of the company and area where the internships were carried out.
• Period and total duration.
• General objective of the residency: what problem or organizational need was addressed?
• Brief description of the report structure.
Length: 1–2 pages.

company_description.title: Company Description
company_description.guidance:
Present the organization where you did the internship:
• Full name, company name and business line.
• Brief history and mission/vision.
• General organizational chart (you can insert a figure).
• Area or department where you worked and its function within the company.
• Technological infrastructure relevant to your activities.
Don't copy the company's website verbatim — paraphrase and cite the source.

activities.title: Activities developed
activities.guidance:
Describe chronologically or by project the activities you carried out:
• For each activity: objective, description of the process, tools or technologies used.
• Include screenshots, diagrams or tables when they support the explanation.
• Mention the challenges encountered and how you resolved them.
• You can organize by weeks, sprints, project phases or work areas.
This is the longest section of the report — be specific and technical.

results.title: Results and contributions
results.guidance:
Present the specific products and contributions of your residence:
• Completed deliverables (systems, reports, manuals, process improvements).
• Metrics or evidence of impact where possible (time saved, errors reduced, etc.).
• Developed professional skills.
• Comparison between the proposed objectives and what was achieved.
Be objective: if something was not concluded, explain why.

conclusions.title: Conclusions
conclusions.guidance:
Close the report with a professional reflection:
• Were the residency objectives met?
• What professional learning did you obtain?
• How did the experience complement your academic training?
• Recommendations for future practitioners or for the company.
Length: 1–2 pages.

references.title: References
references.guidance:
List the sources consulted during the practices: technical manuals, standards, articles, websites.
The list is automatically generated from your .bib.
APA Style 7. Use the DOI importer to easily add academic references.

appendices.title: Annexes
appendices.guidance:
Includes support material that would be very extensive in the main body:
• Letter of acceptance from the company.
• Letter of completion/evaluation from the business tutor.
• Weekly logs (if required by your institution).
• Relevant source code.
• User or technical manuals developed.
• Photographic evidence of the workplace.
Number each annex (Annex A, B…) and refer to them from the text.
